name: Possession
description: Possession is the cross-cultural belief and reported experience that a human body and its functions can be controlled by an external agent — a spirit, ghost, demon, deity, or ancestor — producing dramatic changes in voice, behavior, language, and apparent identity. It is documented in 74% of 488 societies surveyed in a 1969 NIMH cross-cultural study.
full_description: Possession is an altered state of consciousness, and the associated behaviors, that practitioners and witnesses attribute to the takeover of a human body by spirits, ghosts, demons, deities, or ancestors. Anthropologist Erika Bourguignon's landmark 1969 NIMH-supported cross-cultural survey identified beliefs in possession in 74% of 488 societies sampled, with the highest prevalence in the Pacific and the lowest among Native American societies. Traditions vary widely: in many African, Afro-diasporic, Hindu, and Pacific contexts possession is sought, ritualized, and integrated with healing or worship; in Christianity and much of Islam it is regarded as an unwanted attack to be addressed through exorcism; in the Jewish kabbalistic tradition the dybbuk is a disembodied soul to be expelled. Notable cases include the witch trials at Loudun (1632–1638), the Salem witch trials (1692), the Watseka Wonder (Lurancy Vennum, 1877–1878), the Roland Doe case (1949) that inspired The Exorcist, and the death of Anneliese Michel (1976) following a Catholic exorcism. Modern psychiatric frameworks classify many possession experiences under the dissociative disorders: the DSM-5 includes 'dissociative trance' and 'possession-form dissociative identity disorder' presentations, while the ICD treats possession trance as a distinct diagnosis when culturally non-normative and distressing.

aliases.name: Demonic possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a malevolent spirit, in Christian and Islamic frameworks

aliases.name: Dybbuk possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a disembodied human soul

origin: Beliefs in and reports of possession are found in the great majority of human societies. Bourguignon's 1969 cross-cultural survey identified some form of possession belief in 74% of 488 societies, with highest prevalence in the Pacific and lowest among Native American societies.

etymology.origin: Latin possessio ('a holding, occupation') via Anglo-Norman; in religious contexts 'possession' translates a range of vernacular and scriptural terms (Greek daimonizesthai 'to be demonized', Hebrew dybbuk 'attachment', Arabic mass al-jinn 'touching of jinn').
etymology.meaning: A holding, occupation, or control of a person by an outside agent
etymology.first_use: Medieval Latin Christian usage; English religious texts from the 14th century onwards

timeline.event: Loudun possessions begin among Ursuline nuns in France
timeline.significance: One of the most studied early-modern possession episodes; Urbain Grandier executed 1634
timeline.source: Wikipedia: Loudun possessions; de Certeau, M. (1970)

timeline.event: Salem witch trials in Massachusetts, fuelled in part by alleged possession of young accusers
timeline.significance: Foundational American case of possession framing in legal proceedings

timeline.event: Watseka Wonder begins: Lurancy Vennum (Watseka, Illinois) reports being possessed by the deceased Mary Roff
timeline.significance: Classic American Spiritualist case studied by E. Winchester Stevens
timeline.source: Stevens, E. W. (1879), The Watseka Wonder

timeline.event: Roland Doe / Robbie Mannheim exorcism in Maryland and Missouri
timeline.significance: Inspiration for William Peter Blatty's The Exorcist (novel 1971, film 1973)

timeline.event: Erika Bourguignon's NIMH-supported cross-cultural survey reports possession beliefs in 74% of 488 societies
timeline.significance: Foundational quantitative anthropological study of possession
timeline.source: Bourguignon, E. (1973), Religion, Altered States of Consciousness, and Social Change

timeline.event: Death of Anneliese Michel in Klingenberg, Bavaria, following 67 Catholic exorcism sessions
timeline.significance: Two priests and the parents convicted of negligent manslaughter; inspired The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) and Requiem (2006)

timeline.event: DSM-III introduces dissociative-disorder diagnoses that overlap with possession presentations
timeline.significance: Formalises a clinical category alongside religious framings

timeline.event: DSM-5 includes possession-form presentations within dissociative identity disorder and dissociative trance disorder
timeline.significance: Recognises culturally framed possession states in mainstream psychiatry

related.description: Ritual response to possession across multiple religious traditions

related.name: Spirit mediumship
related.description: Voluntary, ritually framed possession in Spiritualist, Afro-diasporic, and other contexts

related.name: Dissociative identity disorder
related.description: Psychiatric framework that overlaps with possession-form presentations

related.name: Jinn
related.description: Islamic spirit category implicated in possession (mass al-jinn)

related.name: Dybbuk
related.description: Possession by a disembodied human soul in Jewish tradition

cultural_notes: Across many traditions, possession is treated as real and consequential; responses range from ritual welcome (mediumship) through containment and accommodation to forceful expulsion (exorcism).
